title: A mastery approach
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart sets out the drivers of and barriers to a mastery approach in primary schools, starting from the belief that every child can learn well given the right support and adequate time. He argues that change begins with surfacing and aligning staff beliefs about learning, since colleagues adopt new beliefs only when they see them contributing to success. Using Harry Fletcher-Wood's responsive teaching model and Mark McCourt's mastery model, he stresses well-sequenced curricula, checking prerequisites before a unit begins, and treating time rather than coverage as the key variable. When children do not understand, he calls for forensic diagnosis followed by corrective teaching within normal curriculum time, with targeted interventions held to strict conditions: matched to need, faithful to the curriculum, run by trained staff, time-limited by progress and not a compensation for weak teaching. He argues that 'falling behind' should be noticed through everyday formative assessment rather than infrequent tests, and that parents should be activated as primary educators. He names bloated curricula, weak curriculum design expertise, the coverage conveyor belt and poorly deployed adults as the main barriers.
points: A mastery approach rests first on shared staff beliefs about children and learning, and those beliefs shift only when colleagues see them producing success.

Hart treats time, not coverage, as the key variable, and calls holding the school to account for every child's learning instead of letting the curriculum conveyor belt roll on a brave but necessary move.
Checking prerequisites before a unit is framed as the most important point of responsive teaching, since gaps there set children up to fall further behind.
Interventions must match a real need, stay faithful to the curriculum, be run by trained adults, end on progress rather than the calendar, and never compensate for weak classroom teaching.
Falling behind should be spotted through day-to-day formative assessment; waiting for standardised test results means acting far too late.
quotes: School systems and collective beliefs enable or hinder children’s learning on a continuum and our role is to keep nudging systems and beliefs in the right direction.

For colleagues to change or adopt new beliefs, they need to see them as contributing to success. And for colleagues to be successful, we need collective understanding and the right systems to enable collective action.
Without secure understanding of prerequisites, children are set up to fail in the upcoming unit of work and beyond, falling further and further behind.
It is a brave but necessary move to hold ourselves to account for every child learning what we intend for them instead of allowing the curriculum conveyor belt to roll on.
Our schools are full of systems and conditions that actively work against this mastery approach. Bloated curricula. A lack of curriculum design expertise.
First and foremost is the tenet that interventions are not a way of compensating for teaching that is not good enough in the first place.

As such, noticing through assessment that a child is struggling has to be based on the information that teachers gather as a matter of course through day to day formative assessment and not rely on more formal assessments captured far less frequently.
